catalog_quote: 2.1.2.1 The Middle Chinese tones The ‘four tones’ (sì shēng 四 聲) of Middle Chinese are píng 平, shǎng 上, qù 去, and rù 入. In our notation they are marked as follows; the English glosses have become conventional translations for the names of the tones: (10) 平 píng < bjaeng ‘level’ no mark 上 shǎng < dzyangX ‘rising’ marked by final -X 去 qù < khjoH ‘departing’ marked by final -H 入 rù < nyip ‘entering’ marked by final -p, -t, or -k The names of the tones were evidently chosen to be both descriptive of the tones they denote and examples of them; thus 平 píng < bjaeng itself is a píngshēng word, 上 shàng ~ shǎng < dzyangX is a shǎngshēng word, and so forth. ... tone_statements.quote: No tonal contrast ever obtains in syllables ending in oral stops: these are always in the Entering tone. In other words, there were only three contrastive tones in Middle Chinese: the Entering ‘tone’ consisted of all the syllables ending in oral stops, on which no tonal contrasts occurred. [...] The choice of these labels has fuelled numerous speculations concerning the phonetic nature of Early Middle Chinese tones: thus it is often assumed that the Level tone was level in pitch, and that the Rising tone was rising. Beyond these rather plausible assumptions, however, it s difficult to go with certainty.

tone_statements.quote: It is controversial whether the so-called "entering-tones" should be included as one of the tone classes of Ancient Chinese. ... tone_statements.quote: Maspero noticed that the four tones of Middle Chinese 65 are not evenly distributed among sets of words written with the same phonetic element ... The píng and shǎng tones on the one hand, and the rù tone on the other, are never found in the same series. This is not surprising, since the rù tone is the only one [of the three] that occurs on words ending in -p, -t or -k, while the píng and shǎng tones occur on open syllables, or syllables ending in sonorant consonants. But the qù tone appears in series of both of these categories. ... 65. In the Tang period, according to the rhyme dictionaries, Chinese only had four tones. The loss of the voicing contrast doubled the number of tones ...

sources.note: Sets out the four traditional EMC tone categories (ping/shang/qu/ru), their phonotactics (Table 1: ru = all and only stop-final syllables, so only three contrastive tones on sonorant-final syllables), states that the phonetic values beyond 'Level = level, Rising = rising' cannot be established with certainty, gives the register split by initial voicing (yin/yang) as the source of modern 6-10-tone systems, and argues the tonogenetic origin: Rising < OC final glottal stop, Departing < OC final -s (> -h), Level = unmarked, following Haudricourt 1954 and Mei 1970; no stress statement.
